content.title: Vote: Which was your favorite WTA 1000 title run of 2026?
content.description: The 2026 WTA 1000 season is in the books, with nine players crowned champions across 10 tournaments. Vote for your favorite title run here.

How craft and consistency fueled Karolina Muchova’s dominant week in Doha

content.body:
The 2026 WTA 1000 season is in the books, with nine players crowned champions across 10 tournaments.

Four of those lifted a WTA 1000 trophy for the first time; five added to existing hauls at this level. From injury comebacks to surges in form, from home-soil glory to historic feats, each title run marked a riveting chapter in the WTA's year. But which was your favorite? Rewind through the champions' best points, then have your say below.

1. Karolina Muchova, Doha

R1: d. Jaqueline Cristian 6-2, 6-3
R2: d. [Q] Tereza Valentova 6-1, 6-4
R3: d. Karolina Pliskova 5-2, ret.
QF: d. Anna Kalinskaya 6-3, 6-4
SF: d. Maria Sakkari 3-6, 6-4, 6-1
F: d. [10] Victoria Mboko 6-4, 7-5

No. 14 seed Muchova snapped a title drought stretching back over six years to lift her second career trophy (following Seoul 2019), and the first at WTA 1000 level, at the Qatar TotalEnergies Open. It foreshadowed a career-best season for the Czech that's also included a second Grand Slam final appearance at Wimbledon and a third title in Bad Homburg. Muchova's defeat of Victoria Mboko in the final was the third of six Top 10 wins she has scored so far in 2026 -- her highest number in a single season.

2. Jessica Pegula, Dubai

R1: bye
R2: d. [Q] Varvara Gracheva 6-4, 6-0
R3: d. [16] Iva Jovic 6-4, 6-2
QF: d. [12] Clara Tauson 6-3, 2-6, 6-4
SF: d. [2] Amanda Anisimova 1-6, 6-4, 6-3
F: d. [7] Elina Svitolina 6-2, 6-4

No. 4 seed Pegula won her fourth career WTA 1000 tournament at the Dubai Duty Free Tennis Championships, and her 10th title overall. The American claimed two of her seven Top 10 wins of 2026 so far en route to the trophy, including a comeback from 6-1, 2-0 down in the semifinals against Amanda Anisimova.

3. Aryna Sabalenka, Indian Wells

R1: bye
R2: d. [Q] Himeno Sakatsume 6-4, 6-2
R3: d. Jaqueline Cristian 6-4, 6-1
R4: d. [16] Naomi Osaka 6-2, 6-4
QF: d. [10] Victoria Mboko 7-6(0), 6-4
SF: d. [14] Linda Noskova 6-3, 6-4
F: d. [3] Elena Rybakina 3-6, 6-3, 7-6(6)

After two previous losses in the BNP Paribas Open final in 2023 and 2025, No. 1 seed Sabalenka claimed her first Indian Wells title after saving one championship point in the final against Elena Rybakina -- avenging her loss to the Kazakhstani player in the Australian Open final. Sabalenka scored two of her seven Top 10 wins of 2026 so far en route to the trophy.

4. Aryna Sabalenka, Miami

R1: bye
R2: d. Ann Li 7-6(5), 6-4
R3: d. Caty McNally 6-4, 6-2
R4: d. [23] Zheng Qinwen 6-3, 6-4
QF: d. Hailey Baptiste 6-4, 6-4
SF: d. [3] Elena Rybakina 6-4, 6-3
F: d. [4] Coco Gauff 6-2, 4-6, 6-3

No. 1 seed Sabalenka became the fifth woman in the Open Era to successfully complete the Sunshine Double after following her Indian Wells title by defending her Miami Open crown. She notched another pair of Top 10 wins along the way, and the two consecutive trophies spearheaded her third career-best 15-match winning streak.

5. Marta Kostyuk, Madrid

R1: bye
R2: d. Yulia Putintseva 6-1, 6-3
R3: d. [5] Jessica Pegula 6-1, 6-4
R4: d. Caty McNally 6-2, 6-3
QF: d. [13] Linda Noskova 7-6(1), 6-0
SF: d. [LL] Anastasia Potapova 6-2, 1-6, 6-1
F: d. [9] Mirra Andreeva 6-3, 7-5

No. 26 seed Kostyuk compiled a 17-match clay-court winning streak, the longest at tour level this year, that included her first career WTA 1000 trophy at the Mutua Madrid Open. It also enabled the Ukrainian, who began the season at No. 26, to make her Top 10 debut in September. Kostyuk notched two of her eight Top 10 wins of 2026 so far in Madrid.

6. Elina Svitolina, Rome

R1: bye
R2: d. [Q] Noemi Basiletti 6-1, 6-3
R3: d. [32] Hailey Baptiste 6-1, 6-2
R4: d. [LL] Nikola Bartunkova 6-2, 6-3
QF: d. [2] Elena Rybakina 2-6, 6-4, 6-4
SF: d. [4] Iga Swiatek 6-4, 2-6, 6-2
F: d. [3] Coco Gauff 6-4, 6-7(3), 6-2

The Internazionali BNL d'Italia champion in 2017-18, No. 7 seed Svitolina reclaimed the Rome crown for a third time after an eight-year gap. The Ukrainian's battling run culminated in a trio of three-set victories over Top 5 opponents, including a 2-hour, 49-minute final defeat of Coco Gauff -- the longest WTA 1000 final of the season. Svitolina's fifth career WTA 1000 title was also her first since returning from maternity leave in 2023.

7. Iga Swiatek, Toronto

R1: bye
R2: d. Sara Bejlek 6-0, 6-3
R3: d. Viktorija Golubic 6-2, 6-1
R4: d. [10] Marta Kostyuk 3-6, 6-1, 6-2
QF: d. [15] Diana Shnaider 6-2, 6-1
SF: d. [9] Elina Svitolina 6-3, 1-6, 6-3
F: d. [2] Elena Rybakina 6-2, 6-3

No. 7 seed Swiatek snapped a 13-month title drought to lift her first National Bank Open trophy -- meaning that of the 15 biggest tournaments (four majors, 10 WTA 1000s and the WTA Finals) currently on the WTA calendar, the Pole is now only missing three: the Australian Open, Dubai and Wuhan. Swiatek's run included two of her four Top 10 wins of 2026.

8. Coco Gauff, Cincinnati

R1: bye
R2: d. Liudmila Samsonova 2-6, 6-4, 6-1
R3: d. [28] Ann Li 6-1, 7-6(3)
R4: d. [22] Marie Bouzkova 6-3, 6-2
QF: d. [10] Marta Kostyuk 6-2, 6-2
SF: d. Sara Bejlek 6-4, 6-1
F: d. [3] Jessica Pegula 6-2, 6-4

No. 4 seed Gauff claimed the Cincinnati Open crown for the second time (following her 2023 title), marking the first time that she has won a trophy at WTA 1000 level or above multiple times. Gauff's final defeat of Jessica Pegula was her fourth of five Top 10 victories so far this year, and marked the first all-American Cincinnati final since 1970.

9. Zheng Qinwen, Beijing

R1: d. [Q] Shi Han 7-6(6), 4-6, 6-2
R2: d. [15] Anna Kalinskaya 6-7(4), 6-4, 3-0 ret.
R3: d. [18] Marie Bouzkova 7-6(4), 4-6, 7-5
R4: d. Alina Charaeva 6-1, 2-6, 6-4
QF: d. [6] Elina Svitolina 6-3, 7-6(6)
SF: d. [13] Elise Mertens 7-5, 6-2
F: d. [4] Mirra Andreeva 7-5, 6-4

Ranked No. 54 but fresh off a run to the US Open quarterfinals as a qualifier, wild card Zheng became the China Open's first home champion with a battling run that included four three-setters and two Top 10 wins. It marked a spectacular return to form -- and to the Top 30 -- for Zheng, who underwent elbow surgery in July 2025 and whose ranking had slipped to No. 160 in June. She dropped 78 games en route to the title -- the second-most of any tour-level champion in the Open Era, only behind Madison Keys (who conceded 87 games on the way to the 2025 Australian Open title).

10. Maja Chwalinska, Wuhan

R1: d. Mayar Sherif 6-3, 6-2
R2: d. Marie Bouzkova 1-6, 6-1, 6-1
R3: d. [10] Iva Jovic 6-4, 6-1
QF: d. Maria Sakkari 6-0, 3-6, 7-5
SF: d. [7] Iga Swiatek 7-5, 6-1
F: d. Sonay Kartal 2-6, 6-4, 6-2

No. 16 seed Chwalinska's spectacular breakthrough season continued at the Dongfeng • Voyah Wuhan Open as the Pole became just the fourth player to win her maiden tour-level title at WTA 1000 level since the format's inception in 2009. Chwalinska, who started the year ranked No. 146 before becoming the first qualifier to reach the Roland Garros final in the Open Era, made her Top 20 debut following her Wuhan title run, which also included her first career Top 10 win -- over compatriot and childhood friend Iga Swiatek in the semifinals.

content.title: Meet your elite eight: A snapshot of the 2026 WTA Finals field
content.description: It's official -- we have our eight-player WTA Finals singles field. Karolina Muchova qualified on Wednesday, and she will join Elena Rybakina, Aryna Sabalenka, Jessica Pegula, Coco Gauff, Mirra Andreeva, Linda Noskova and Elina Svitolina in Indian Wells.

related.label: Karolina Muchova secures final qualification place for FAGE WTA Finals Indian Wells
Swiatek withdraws from Ningbo, ends season to 'rest and recover'
Vote: Which was your favorite WTA 1000 title run of 2026?

content.body:
Karolina Muchova secured the last WTA Finals qualification berth on Wednesday, and with that we have our elite eight in the desert.

The WTA Finals at Indian Wells will feature three former champions, three newcomers and a wide-open field.

Ahead of the year-end tournament and culmination of the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz season, here's a snapshot of how they got to Indian Wells, and their outlook heading into the finale. 

Elena Rybakina

W-L record: 49-14

Titles won: 3 (Australian Open, Stuttgart, US Open)

Previous WTA Finals appearances: 3

Best WTA Finals result: 2025 champion

The skinny: Rybakina was the best player in the world this year. She burst out of the gate, following up her 2025 WTA Finals sweep with an Australian Open title, and ended the Grand Slam season with another major, at the US Open. She beat Aryna Sabalenka in both finals, and the latter win gave her the No. 1 ranking for the first time, ending Sabalenka's 99-week run at the top. She lost her opening match in Beijing and skipped Wuhan, but is playing this week in Ningbo, the last Finals qualifier still in action before Indian Wells.

READ MORE: A US Open champ and new No. 1, Rybakina completes trifecta with a ticket to WTA Finals

Aryna Sabalenka

W-L record: 47-10

Titles won: 3 (Brisbane, Indian Wells, Miami)

Previous WTA Finals appearances: 5

Best WTA Finals result: Finalist in 2022 and 2025

The skinny: On the surface, a season without a major title for the first time since 2022 might seem disappointing by Sabalenka’s standards. She still won 47 matches, made a pair of Grand Slam finals and won two WTA 1000 tournaments. Those back-to-back titles in Indian Wells and Miami were the high-water mark of her season, as she became just the fifth player in WTA Tour history to sweep the Sunshine Double. She's had her most success on hard courts, and has historically played very well at the Finals, a tournament she's eager to check off her bucket list. 

She enters the Finals with very little momentum, having lost two of three in Asia, but she should be well-rested.

READ MORE: One result at a time, Aryna Sabalenka keeps ending up at the WTA Finals

Mirra Andreeva

W-L record: 50-16

Titles won: 3 (Adelaide, Linz, Roland Garros)

Previous WTA Finals appearances: 0

The skinny: Andreeva has been prolific in 2026, tying Jessica Pegula for the most match-wins (50) on the WTA Tour. The apex of her season was at Roland Garros, where she won her first major. The 19-year-old made four other finals, winning two of them, and her hot hand has continued through the Asian Swing, where she's coming off a run to the final in Beijing. Currently at a career-high No. 3, Andreeva concludes the best season of her career fittingly, at her first WTA Finals. 

READ MORE: '150 percent of your focus': Andreeva on what it will take to compete at the WTA Finals

Jessica Pegula

W-L record: 50-13

Titles won: 2 (Dubai, Charleston)

Previous WTA Finals appearances: 4

Best WTA Finals result: 2023 final

The skinny: Pegula was a model of consistency once again in 2026. Tied with Andreeva for the most match-wins on tour, Pegula had the best winning percentage in the world and made five finals. Her two titles came earlier in the season, in Dubai and Charleston, and since April she's gone title-less, losing three consecutive finals in Berlin, Washington, DC and Cincinnati. Pegula has played just one match since the US Open, and should arrive at Indian Wells refreshed after some weeks off. 

READ MORE: How Jessica Pegula’s discipline earned her another trip to the WTA Finals

Coco Gauff

W-L record: 47-15

Titles won: 1 (Cincinnati)

Previous WTA Finals appearances: 4

Best WTA Finals result: 2024 champion

The skinny: Gauff's season kicked into gear in Miami, where she reached the final, and she made another WTA 1000 final in Rome a month and a half later. There was further heartbreak late in tournaments, with semifinal runs at Wimbledon and in Toronto, before she got her first title of the year in Cincinnati. She followed that up with a semifinal run in New York, in what was a highly productive Hard-Court Swing. Gauff is so dangerous on hard courts, and the 2024 champion will look to rebound after failing to get out of the group stage last year.

READ MORE: By the numbers: Gauff and Pegula are making WTA Finals history one year at a time

Elina Svitolina

W-L record: 46-14

Titles won: 2 (Auckland, Rome)

Previous WTA Finals appearances: 3

Best WTA Finals result: 2018 champion

The skinny: Svitolina returns to the Finals after seven years, and nearly a decade after she made her debut at the year-end tournament.  The 32-year-old won her first 10 matches of the season, including a title in Auckland and a semifinal run in Melbourne, and then won her biggest title of the year on clay, in Rome. She also reached the semis in Indian Wells, Stuttgart and Toronto, to go with a final in Dubai. Back-to-back quarterfinal runs in Beijing and Wuhan show that the 2018 champion is still in form at the tail end of the season. 

READ MORE: WTA Finals flashback: How Svitolina turned a shaky stretch in Asia into the biggest title of her career

Karolina Muchova

W-L record: 40-11

Titles won: 2 (Doha, Bad Homburg)

Previous WTA Finals appearances: 0

The skinny: It's hard to believe that when Muchova won the Qatar TotalEnergies Open in February, it was only her second career title, and first since 2019. It was the biggest title of her career, and it set the tone for the rest of the season, which included a second title in Bad Homburg and a runner-up finish at Wimbledon. That run to the final propelled her to a career-high No. 6 in the world. Muchova also made semifinals in Brisbane and Miami, and a final in Stuttgart. With her all-court game, athleticism and ability to hit any shot from any angle, she's one of the toughest outs in tennis.

READ MORE: Karolina Muchova secures final qualification place for FAGE WTA Finals Indian Wells

Linda Noskova

W-L record: 35-15

Titles won: 2 (Berlin, Wimbledon)

Previous WTA Finals appearances: 0

The skinny: Noskova's breakthrough came at Wimbledon, where she won her first career major as a No. 9 seed. Though the title was surprising, anyone who had been paying attention could see that she was a threat on grass, having beaten Pegula in the Berlin final a couple weeks earlier. But the 21-year-old proved that she can win on all surfaces in 2026, reaching the semis at Indian Wells earlier in the year and the quarterfinals of the US Open in September. Noskova withdrew from Wuhan with a left calf injury, but she should have enough time to recover for Indian Wells.

READ MORE: The first-timers who won the WTA Finals: Could Andreeva or Noskova be next?

content.title: How Jessica Pegula’s discipline earned her another trip to the WTA Finals
content.description: Jessica Pegula has put together the kind of season that doesn’t always make headlines in the moment but looks remarkable in hindsight. Now as she returns to the WTA Finals, she explains how it all came together.

related.label: '150 percent of your focus': Andreeva on what it will take to compete at the WTA Finals
By the numbers: Gauff and Pegula are making WTA Finals history one year at a time
Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff qualify for WTA Finals in Indian Wells

content.body:
By the time Jessica Pegula cracked the top 100 in 2019, at the age of 25, many of the players she competed against had already spent years establishing themselves among the best on tour. Pegula had arrived later than most, but she arrived with momentum, winning her first title that same season.

From there, the ascent was steady and, by the standards of a late start, remarkably quick. Within three years, a then-28-year-old Pegula had climbed to a career-high No. 3 and earned her first trip to the WTA Finals, a rise that turned a late start into a defining part of her story rather than a limitation.

Now, four years on from that first appearance, the current World No. 4 remains among the game’s best, and she is preparing for a fifth consecutive WTA Finals, this time at Indian Wells.

For Pegula, the streak is something she is still wrapping her head around. Making the year-end finals five years in a row is “pretty crazy,” she told wtatennis.com in Wuhan, and it is a run she admits she never imagined was possible. To her, it stands as proof “that things can change, you can really improve as a player mentally, physically, on court.”

She points to the mental strength it took to handle the ups and downs of each season, along with her ability to stay healthy and put herself in position to win a lot of matches year after year.

“It’s an honor and definitely a huge achievement for me,” she said.

Pegula's rise on tour comes down to how her consistency. Early on in her career, it wasn't there. From 2011 to 2017 at the ITF/World Tennis level, Pegula amassed a 51.95% win rate per season (in seasons where she played at least 10 matches). She also never won an ITF/World Tennis title. 

Since 2020 on the WTA Tour Driven by Merdedes-Benz, she's averaging a near 70% win rate. Every year since 2022 -- the year of her first WTA Finals -- she's won at least one title with multiple the past four seasons. Pegula's current 2026 record of 50-14 (78.1%) is her career best winning percentage in a single season to date. 

"Making WTA finals is all about consistency," Pegula said. "To be honest, I'm pretty shocked that it's my fifth year. In the past, I was not a consistent player at all coming up in the in tournaments when I started playing pros. Even when I was starting to do better in the pros, I always felt like my consistency was my worst trait."

Now her consistency is her best trait, particularly over the past year. From the 2025 US Open to her Dubai title in February, she advanced to seven straight semifinals.

WTA Finals Indian Wells bound ✈️ @JPegula has secured her spot on #TheUltimateStage! Get your tickets to see Jessica 🔗 https://t.co/Q9saXxEdt1 https://t.co/4PNlmUIxHP

— wta (@WTA) October 14, 2026

Her next three tournaments brought more of the same, with quarterfinal runs at both Sunshine Double events and a second straight title in Charleston, stretching her streak to 10 consecutive tournaments of at least reaching the last eight.

Pegula also finished runner-up in Cincinnati, Berlin and Washington, reached the semifinals at the US Open for the second year in a row and made the quarterfinals at Wimbledon and Rome.

"I was really happy with my overall level throughout the year, and when I did have any sort of dips, I was able to bounce back really strong," Pegula said. "You're gonna have some bad losses and some bad swings sometimes, but it's always about how you can bounce back and not let that affect you.

"I did that really well at certain points during the year where maybe I felt like I wasn't playing great or I lost a tough match, I was able to kind of go and have a pretty good result pretty soon after, and I think that's one of my strengths."

With her proven track record, Pegula has established herself among the tour’s best eight players. She returns to the year-end event having advanced out of the round robin stage twice, reaching the final in 2023 and the semifinals in 2025.

Her best finish at Indian Wells has been the quarterfinals, which she has reached twice, but with a different format and the chance to compete on home soil, Pegula is ready to return.

“Being able to stay in my home country, I’m always going to appreciate that,” Pegula said.

Indian Wells holds a special place for her, both because she has had good results there and because she feels the fan base is great not just for Americans but for all the players, which she expects to make for a terrific atmosphere.

“I’ve experienced a lot of different places,” she said, “but I’m excited to be back in Indian Wells because it’s such a great tennis town.”
content.summary: Jessica Pegula has put together the kind of season that doesn’t always make headlines in the moment but looks remarkable in hindsight. Now as she returns to the WTA Finals, she explains how it all came together.

content.title: 'In the moment' Ostapenko saves three match points, stuns Pegula in Wuhan
content.description: Jelena Ostapenko saved three match points in the second-set tiebreak to upset Jessica Pegula in the Dongfeng • Voyah Wuhan Open second round.

related.label: Around Wuhan: Muchova's impressive tiebreak feat; Jovic, Chwalinska set to meet
'It feels like it was a century ago': Sakkari recounts 2017 Wuhan breakthrough
By the numbers: Gauff and Pegula are making WTA Finals history one year at a time

content.body:
Jelena Ostapenko pulled off a thrilling turnaround in the Dongfeng • Voyah Wuhan Open second round, saving three match points in the second-set tiebreak to upset No. 2 seed and 2025 runner-up Jessica Pegula 2-6, 7-6(7), 6-3 in 2 hours and 23 minutes.

The result is Ostapenko's third Top 10 win of 2026, and 28th of her career -- and the first time she has beaten a Top 5 opponent since last year's Stuttgart final, where she defeated Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 6-1. It's the third time that she's defeated Pegula in seven meetings dating back to 2015, following her 3-6, 6-2, 7-6(3) win in the 2015 Québec City second round and her 6-4, 6-2 win in the Beijing second round. It's also a revenge of sorts for her 2023 Doha loss, in which Pegula saved two match points for a 6-2, 2-6, 7-5 victory.

Ostapenko will next face either Leylah Fernandez or qualifier Shi Han as she bids to reach her third WTA 1000 quarterfinal of the season.

How did Ostapenko pull off the comeback?

As is often the case with Ostapenko, her ratio of winners to unforced errors can fluctuate from one extreme to the other with little warning. In the first set, she was barely able to stay in longer exchanges, winning just two points when the rally exceeded four shots and committing 11 unforced errors.

The 2017 Roland Garros champion's form ticked up slightly at the setart of the second set, but Pegula kept her foot on the pedal to break for 3-2. Ostapenko received a medical timeout at this juncture and returned to court with her right arm heavily strapped.

"I had a lot of pain in my arm, then I took a painkiller and then I was fighting for every single point," she explained in her on-court interview.

Her form continued to improve as the set drew on -- but even so, Pegula's strategy of giving nothing away enabled her to advance to three match points in the tiebreak. On the first, with the court wide open, the American netted a simple volley. Ostapenko found a service winner on her second serve to save the second, then came up with an audacious drop shot play to save the third.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Surging with confidence, Ostapenko roared through the decider with a scintillating display of her customary power tennis, finishing the match with 46 winners (including 10 aces) to 37 unforced errors (including 11 double faults). Her return of serve was particularly breathtaking -- even when Ostapenko failed to convert a 30-0 lead when serving for the win, she simply recovered to break Pegula in the next game courtesy of two clean return winners.

It wasn't just Ostapenko's first strike that improved as the match went on, though. The Latvian won 23 rallies that went over four shots in the last two sets, including five that went over nine shots.

"The US swing was pretty bad for me," Ostapenko said in her press conference (she went 0-3 in it). "After that, I feel like I was practising well at home. I feel I'm in the right zone now and I feel like I'm doing the right decisions. Sometimes when I have to go for the shots I'm going for it, sometimes -- even when I play very aggressive -- but today some points I was just trying to keep the ball in play and wait for the good ball to attack. I feel like I was doing this really good today, and yesterday, and also in Beijing."

Anatomy of a hot shot: that drop shot down match point

The tried and trusted Ostapenko approach to tennis is to go with power at all times, and then with more power if necessary. Which is what makes her third match point save such a wild decision: after hammering the ball from side to side, unable to break through Pegula's defenses, Ostapenko attempted a drop shot for the first and only time in the match. It landed perfectly for a winner, curving away from Pegula and cut too fine for even her wheels to reach.

What was she thinking? Asked about it afterwards, Ostapenko's grin indicated she knew how unexpected a shot choice it had been.

"Honestly I don't even want to think what I was thinking, because I think I was not thinking anything," she said. "I was just in the moment. I think I play the best when I go by my -- it's funny to say, but with my instincts, with my feelings. I think you don't really have to think what you are doing. Just be in the moment and play tennis."

How many times has Ostapenko won from match point down?

This result is the seventh time that Ostapenko has won from match point down in a WTA main draw, and tied for the most match points she has saved en route to victory:

2016 Cincinnati R1, d. Anna Karolina Schmiedlova 1-6, 7-6(6), 7-6(5) -- saved two
2017 Prague R2, d. Caroline Wozniacki 5-7, 6-3, 7-6(5) -- saved one
2019 Charleston R2, d. Shelby Rogers 4-6, 6-3, 7-6(4) -- saved one
2019 Linz SF, d. Ekaterina Alexandrova 1-6, 7-6(5), 7-5 -- saved three
2022 Seoul R2, d. Anastasia Gasanova 6-3, 5-7, 7-5 -- saved one
2024 Linz R2, d. Clara Tauson 3-6, 6-4, 7-6(7) -- saved one
2026 Wuhan R2, d. Jessica Pegula 2-6, 7-6(7), 6-3 -- saved three
content.author: WTA Staff
content.summary: Jelena Ostapenko saved three match points in the second-set tiebreak to upset Jessica Pegula in the Dongfeng • Voyah Wuhan Open second round.

content.title: By the numbers: Gauff and Pegula are making WTA Finals history one year at a time
content.description: Coco Gauff and Jessica Pegula have been Top 10 fixtures for more than four years, and now they’re headed to a fifth straight WTA Finals. It’s a streak that’s easy to miss, until you look at the numbers.
content.body:
Before the China Open late last month, Coco Gauff told reporters her suitcase was already packed to capacity, and her mother had wondered how the gifts waiting in Beijing would fit. Gauff’s solution was to pack an extra bag, a modest but telling bit of foresight considering that her season, as it has for years, will stretch into the final week of the tour calendar.

On Wednesday, Gauff learned she won't be unpacking for a while. She and fellow American Jessica Pegula each secured a place at the WTA Finals in Indian Wells, a fifth consecutive appearance for both. The season-ending event is familiar territory by now, and each return adds to a number of milestones that are easy to overlook.

Gauff and Pegula have spent years at the top of the sport together, and string of success that is anything but a happy accident. Few players from the same country have shared the Top 10 for this long, and few have matched it with a run of year-end appearances like theirs. Together, they have become one of the most dominant duos from a single country the sport has seen in decades.

Their excellence has become so habitual that you’d be forgiven for overlooking their accomplishments. Showing up atop the rankings week after week and ultimately solidifying a spot in the season-ending field year after year has started to feel like the natural order of things, when in fact the sport has seen very little like it. Here is some statistical perspective: 

Rankings staying power

209 consecutive weeks together in the singles Top 10
Pegula and Gauff have held Top 10 rankings simultaneously for 209 straight weeks. That is more than four years among the sport's leading players, long enough to span multiple seasons without a single weekly update breaking the run.

222 weeks for Pegula, 209 for Gauff
Pegula's individual Top 10 streak stands at 222 consecutive weeks, 13 more than Gauff's. Gauff's entire streak overlaps with their shared run. Pegula reached the Top 10 earlier and has stayed there since.

Four same-country pairs with 200-plus weeks together
Since 1997, only four pairs from the same country have each spent at least 200 consecutive weeks in the Top 10 together:

  • Arantxa Sánchez Vicario and Conchita Martínez: 319 weeks
  • Lindsay Davenport and Venus Williams: 241 weeks
  • Serena and Venus Williams: 224 weeks
  • Coco Gauff and Jessica Pegula: 209 weeks

Gauff and Pegula are the first same-country pair to reach 200 weeks since the Williams sisters did it in 2003.

WTA Finals pedigree

Five straight WTA Finals appearances
Both players will make a fifth consecutive appearance, covering 2022 through 2026. They are the first American pair to qualify together for five straight editions since Mary Joe Fernandez and Zina Garrison from 1989 to 1993, and the first same-country pair to match that streak since Frenchwomen Nathalie Tauziat and Sandrine Testud appeared together from 1997 to 2001.

Five Americans with longer individual streaks
Five Americans have strung together more consecutive appearances than Pegula and Gauff's five. Martina Navratilova leads with 17, followed by Garrison with 12, Davenport with nine, Pam Shriver with seven and Chris Evert with six. Navratilova represented Czechoslovakia in her first two appearances.

Both have found success at the Finals, most memorably in 2024, when Gauff beat Zheng Qinwen in the championship match to capture the title. Pegula has had her own deep runs, reaching the final in 2023 and the semifinals in 2025, and now the two return to Indian Wells together once more.
content.author: Matt Wilansky
content.summary: Coco Gauff and Jessica Pegula have been Top 10 fixtures for more than four years, and now they’re headed to a fifth straight WTA Finals. It’s a streak that’s easy to miss, until you look at the numbers.

content.title: Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff qualify for WTA Finals in Indian Wells
content.description: Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff punched their tickets to the season-ending event in November, making it five straight appearances for both American stars.
content.body:
• Both players will be appearing at the season-ending event for the fifth consecutive year
  • Gauff is a former WTA Finals champion, lifting the title in 2024
  • Pegula has reached an impressive five finals this season, including two at WTA 1000 level

  • Tickets are available here for this year's WTA Finals at the Indian Wells Tennis Garden

The WTA announced Wednesday American stars Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff will be competing on tennis' ultimate stage in November as both players have secured qualification for the WTA Finals Indian Wells.

Pegula and Gauff will each make their fifth consecutive appearance at the season-ending tournament. They join PIF WTA World No. 1 Elena Rybakina, Indian Wells and Miami champion Aryna Sabalenka, Roland-Garros winner Mirra Andreeva and Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova, with two singles spots still open.

Pegula and Gauff’s qualification means the WTA Finals singles draw will feature multiple American players for the fifth consecutive year.

Pegula is no stranger to the WTA Finals and across her four previous appearances finished as runner-up in 2023 and made the semifinals in 2025.

Her season has been highlighted by reaching an impressive five finals, including two at WTA 1000 level, winning the Dubai Duty Free Tennis Championships and contesting the title match at the Cincinnati Open.

The Buffalo native also reached the final at three WTA 500 tournaments, winning the Credit One Charleston Open and finishing runner-up at the VANDA Pharmaceuticals Berlin Tennis Open and the Mubadala DC Open in Washington, D.C.

Florida's Coco Gauff has also flourished this season at WTA 1000 events, winning the Cincinnati Open and reaching the final at the Miami Open presented by Itaú and Internazionali BNL d'Italia (Rome).

The former WTA Finals champion, who in 2024 became the first American player to win the title in 10 years, also performed strongly at the Grand Slams to bolster her qualification hopes, reaching the semifinals at Wimbledon and the US Open and the quarterfinals at the Australian Open.

The WTA Finals Indian Wells field includes eight singles players and eight doubles teams from the PIF Race to the WTA Finals Leaderboard. The top seven in each race qualify automatically. The eighth spot goes to the highest-ranked Grand Slam champion, singles player or doubles team, ranked from No. 8 to No. 20 who has not already qualified.

 This showcases the world’s best singles players and doubles teams competing in a round-robin format with the singles champion lifting the WTA Finals Billie Jean King Trophy and the doubles champions earning the WTA Finals Martina Navratilova Trophy. The prestigious season-ending tournament celebrates the best of the WTA on and off the court, delivering an unrivalled fan experience that blends sport, entertainment, and culture.

Tickets are available here for this year's WTA Finals at the Indian Wells Tennis Garden, one of the sport's premier destinations and tournament locations.

content.title: 'Back to normal': Pegula ready for late-season push in Wuhan
content.description: Jessica Pegula returns to the Asian swing feeling healthy and motivated to finish the 2026 season strong, with a Wuhan title and a spot in the WTA Finals in her sights.

related.label: Zheng Qinwen makes history with China Open win in first title since 2024
Best of Wuhan media day: Top quotes and Kostyuk, Eala's adventures
Noskova pulls out of Wuhan with left calf injury

content.body:
Jessica Pegula may be getting a late start to her Asian swing, but the top-ranked American still has plenty to play for in the final weeks of the 2026 WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz season.

Sidelined since reaching the US Open semifinals after what she called a “long summer,” Pegula said she is healthy again and motivated to finish the year strong. She reached at least the semifinals in three of the four tournaments she played during the hard-court stretch following Wimbledon, ending with a loss to Aryna Sabalenka in New York.

Afterward, Pegula, 32, acknowledged the physical toll of her schedule and withdrew from Singapore and Beijing. She returns this week at the Dongfeng · Voyah Wuhan Open, where she is the defending finalist.

“Sometimes things can happen because of the accumulation of a lot of matches, playing a lot of tennis,” Pegula said ahead of the event.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by 2026 DONGFENG •VOYAH WUHAN OPEN (@wuhanopenwta)

"When a big tournament finally ends, I think sometimes, for me at least, I start feeling a little bit run down. For me to balance how I'm feeling physically and mentally, it's always to know when I'm at that threshold and maybe it's time to let my body recover and catch up to all the activity and adrenaline that I was going through for the last few months."

Now feeling "back to normal" after several weeks of routine at home with husband Taylor Gahagen and their three dogs, Pegula is ready to make the most of her remaining tournaments, though she has yet to officially secure a place at the WTA Finals.

Currently No. 3 in the Race to the WTA Finals, Pegula said she always intended to return to Wuhan, where she'll look to build momentum ahead of a potential fifth consecutive appearance at the year-end championships.

"I think competing at a WTA 1000 is always a good time to win the tournament and to try to do your best," she said. "I didn't necessarily want to skip Beijing, so for me, coming back to Wuhan was something I always planned to do."

Seeded No. 2 in Wuhan, Pegula opens against the winner of Jelena Ostapenko and Daria Kasatkina.

content.title: Rybakina, Pegula, Svitolina, Swiatek headline Tokyo field
content.description: World No. 1 Elena Rybakina will be the top seed at the Toray Pan Pacific Open in Tokyo, and she'll be joined by Top 10 players Jessica Pegula, Elina Svitolina, Iga Swiatek and Marta Kostyuk.

related.label: Elena Rybakina settles into Beijing as No. 1 after a whirlwind stretch

content.body:
World No. 1 Elena Rybakina will be the top seed at next month's Toray Pan Pacific Open in Tokyo, the final 500-level tournament of the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz season.

She'll be joined by fellow Top 10 players Jessica Pegula, Elina Svitolina, Iga Swiatek and Marta Kostyuk.

As the last WTA 500 of the season, the Toray Pan Pacific Open will potentially carry significant WTA Finals implications. 

Svitolina and Karolina Muchova are currently six and seventh, respectively, on the PIF Race to the WTA Finals leaderboard. Linda Noskova is eighth, though because she has won a Grand Slam this season, she'd have to finish below No. 20 on the leaderboard not to qualify.

Kostyuk and Swiatek are ninth and 10th, respectively, on the leaderboard as the second-to-last WTA 1000 in Beijing is getting underway.

The Tokyo field will also include Top 20 players Belinda Bencic, Iva Jovic, Diana Shnaider, Sorana Cirstea (in what could potentially be the final tournament of her career), Naomi Osaka, Alexandra Eala, Elise Mertens and Jasmine Paolini.

The final four direct entrants are Maja Chwalinska, Anna Kalinskaya, Leylah Fernandez and Ekaterina Alexandrova.

The first four main-draw alternates are Ann Li, Diane Parry, Maria Sakkari and Nikola Bartunkova.

In addition to the 17 direct entrants, the 28-player field includes six qualifiers, four wild cards and a special exempt spot. The top four seeds will receive byes into the second round.

Bencic is the defending champion in Tokyo. She defeated Varvara Gracheva, Muchova and Sofia Kenin in her first three matches before beating Noskova in the final. This will be her seventh time playing the Toray Pan Pacific Open. She made her debut here in 2013, and reached the final two years later, falling to Agnieszka Radwanska. 

Osaka is also a former champion in Tokyo, winning this tournament back in 2019. She also made finals here in 2016 and 2018.

Rybakina, who is also playing for the year-end No. 1 ranking, won two matches here last year before pulling out of the semifinals with back pain.

First-round action in Tokyo will begin on Monday, Oct. 26, and the tournament will run through Sunday, Nov. 1, when both the singles and doubles finals will be played. 

In addition to 500 ranking points, the Tokyo champion will earn $185,500.

content.title: Pegula, defending champion Anisimova pull out of China Open with injuries
content.description: World No. 3 Jessica Pegula and defending champion Amanda Anisimova have withdrawn from the China Open in Beijing as a result of continuing injuries. Marta Kostyuk and Sorana Cirstea have also pulled out of the event.

related.label: The votes are in: Alexandra Eala is your Star of the Hard-Court Swing
Muchova, Noskova send Czechia into Billie Jean King Cup final
The 2026 Hard-Court Swing stats wrap: Longest matches, MP saves and more

content.body:
BEIJING -- World No. 3 Jessica Pegula and defending champion Amanda Anisimova have withdrawn from the upcoming 2026 China Open in Beijing, citing ongoing injuries.

In addition, World No. 10 Marta Kostyuk and No. 15 Sorana Cirstea are also out of the event.

The World No. 11 Anisimova has been dealing with a left wrist injury that forced her to pull out of the ongoing Singapore Tennis Open. As for Pegula, her injury was unspecified, but she similarly withdrew from Singapore ahead of the tournament. 

After their withdrawals from Singapore, Beijing was expected to be their first appearances since the US Open, where Pegula advanced to the final four while Anisimova exited in the third round. Kostyuk played in Guadalajara following the US Open, while Cirstea has not competed since New York. 

“I’m so sad not to be in Beijing this year, but I need to focus on recovering from an injury," Anisimova said in a statement. "The fans in Beijing always give amazing support, so I can’t wait to be back next year.”

Last year in Beijing, Anisimova won her second career WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz 1000 title to become the third American to hoist the China Open trophy. She defeated Linda Noskova, who edged out Pegula reached the semifinals in a tight three-set thriller. 

On her way to the final, Anisimova also defeated Katie Boulter, Zhang Shaui, Karolina Muchova, Jasmine Paolini and Coco Gauff, earning three top 15 wins at the time. 

Anisimova, Pegula, Kostyuk and Cirstea join Madison Keys (abdominal injury), McCartney Kessler (hip), Zhang (change of schedule), Karolina Pliskova (back), Emma Raducanu (leg) and Hanne Vandewinkel (illness) as pre-tournament singles withdrawals in Beijing. 

The China Open main draw will begin Wednesday, Sept. 30, with qualifying held on Sept. 28-29. The tournament features a 96-player singles field and is the second-to-last WTA 1000 of the season.

content.title: 50 days until the WTA Finals, these 3 burning questions need answers
content.description: Only 50 days remain until the year-end WTA Finals at Indian Wells. Here's what to watch for, and what's at stake, as we edge close and closer to the premier tournament on the WTA calendar.

related.label: Rybakina to miss Billie Jean King Cup quarterfinals in Shenzhen
Singapore 411: Dates, draws, schedule, prize money and more
Rybakina, Sabalenka, Pegula, Gauff headline Wuhan field

content.body:
We're officially 50 days out from the year-end WTA Finals, which will be contested at the iconic Indian Wells Tennis Garden. 

The premier tournament on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz calendar, the WTA Finals features the top eight singles players and top eight doubles teams, pitting them against each other in a round-robin format to crown a WTA champion.

As we enter the final stretch of the season, only one singles player has qualified for the Finals. Elena Rybakina, who currently leads the PIF WTA Race to the Finals with 7,492 points, qualified after winning the US Open.

Aryna Sabalenka is currently in second, with 6,485 points, and Jessica Pegula (5,825), Coco Gauff (5,654) and Mirra Andreeva (5,614) round out the top five. Elina Svitolina (4,809), Karolina Muchova (4,400) and Linda Noskova (4,234) would have the final three slots, if the season ended today.

But the season isn't ending today. In fact, after the Hard-Court Swing concludes in Guadalajara and Sao Paolo this weekend, there are still eight tournaments that count towards the Finals race. Two of those tournaments, which will be of most consequence to the leaderboard, are back-to-back WTA 1000s in Beijing and Wuhan.

Ahead of the season's culmination in Indian Wells, as we shift our focus to the Asian Swing, here are three burning questions about Finals qualification and the year-end rankings.

1. Which players on the outside looking in have the best chance to qualify?

Noskova is in excellent standing to qualify, despite being in the eighth spot. As a Grand Slam champion this year, she'd have to fail below No. 20 on the leaderboard not to qualify. That means even if Noskova struggles during the Asian Swing and drops several spots, she'd still be headed to Indian Wells.

With Noskova in firm position, the two players currently on the outside looking in -- Marta Kostyuk and Iga Swiatek -- are chasing Muchova and Svitolina. No. 9 Kostyuk (3,850 points) currently trails Muchova and Svitolina by 550 points and 950 points, respectively. Swiatek (3,584 points) trails Muchova by 816 points and Svitolina by 1,225 points. 

Kostyuk pulled out of next week's Billie Jean King Cup quarterfinal, citing the need for additional recovery time for her injured wrist, though she's still currently scheduled to play Beijing and Wuhan. She earned 108 points by reaching the quarterfinals in Guadalajara this week, after Taylor Townsend pulled out before their match, but missed an opportunity to earn more after falling to Liudmila Samsonova in her next match.

Kostyuk played only the two WTA 1000s during last year's Asian Swing, going just 2-2 across Beijing and Wuhan, so she'll need much stronger results there next month to sneak into the final eight. She'll also likely have to play additional tournaments during the swing. There are three 500 tournaments left on the schedule, though she's not playing the first one, next week's Singapore Tennis Open. Last year, Rybakina won six straight matches at WTA 500s, including a title in Ningbo, to sneak into the WTA Finals field.

As for Swiatek, she is the defending champion in Seoul, though she won't be there this year after that tournament was changed from a 500 to a 250. She had modest runs at the Asian WTA 1000s last year, reaching the Round of 16 in Beijing and the quarterfinals in Wuhan, but will have to go deeper this fall. 

Swiatek is a former champion in Beijing, though she won it back in 2023. 

2) Who will finish the season as the year-end No. 1?

Sabalenka, currently second in the PIF WTA Race to the Finals, is on the doorstep of qualification. In fact, she would have qualified with a win in the US Open final. So there's no drama there.

There is drama, however, when it comes to the year-end No. 1 ranking, which Sabalenka has finished with each of the last two years. 

The PIF WTA Rankings race is different than the PIF WTA Race to the Finals, as rankings points have to be defended from the season prior. Currently, No. 2 Sabalenka trails No. 1 Sabalenka by a healthy 2,026 points in the PIF WTA Rankings.

Sabalenka, who hasn't won a title since Miami in March, didn't play the China Open last year, so there's ample opportunity in Beijing next month. She'll be defending 390 points in Wuhan, where she reached the semifinals in 2025. She'll be further boosted if she decides to play one of the two WTA 500 events after Wuhan.

Rybakina played far more during the Asian Swing, though the points she's defending at the 1000s are reasonable after reaching the third round in Beijing and then the quarterfinals in Wuhan. It was after that that she got red hot, with a title in Ningbo and a semifinal run in Tokyo. Should she play those events, she could potentially drop points with lesser performances.

It could very well come down to the WTA Finals, where Rybakina is defending 1,500 points as the defending undefeated champion. She defeated Sabalenka, fittingly, in the final last year. Wouldn't it be something if they met again at that stage, for the year-end No. 1 ranking?

One thing to keep an eye on is Rybakina's health. After suffering a left ankle injury in Cincinnati last month, she didn't play for a week and said it hurt to walk. She looked healthy at the US Open, but has pulled out of next week's Billie Jean King Cup quarterfinals to rest and recover further.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

3. Which American will be ranked highest at the end of the year?

Like Sabalenka, Pegula and Gauff have a clear look at the basket at No. 3 and No. 4, respectively, on the PIF WTA Race to the Finals leaderboard, and should qualify for the Finals assuming they play to their standard in Asia.

But who outranks the other at the end of the year remains in question. Gauff was the highest-ranked American at the end of last year, finishing No. 3 ahead of No. 4 Amanda Anisimova and No. 6 Pegula.

Pegula has made inroads since then. She's currently the highest-ranked American, at No. 3, but only by a smidgen. Gauff, ranked fourth, trails Pegula by a minuscule 21 points. They both held serve at the US Open, reaching the semifinals in New York, but Gauff will have more points to defend in Asia. She took nine of 10 matches at the back-to-back 1000s last year, getting to the semifinals in Beijing before winning the title in Wuhan. She has traditionally played some of her best tennis at those tournaments, and she'll need to be almost perfect again not to lose points.

That doesn't mean it will be easy for Pegula to catch her, though. The 32-year-old also had a terrific Asian Swing last year, albeit slightly worse, reaching the semis in Beijing and then the final in Wuhan (where she lost to Gauff). That final, it turns out, gave Gauff the slight points edge during the swing. 

Like the quest for year-end No. 1, it will very likely come down to the WTA Finals. Gauff will have a chance to make a push there, assuming she qualifies, after not getting out of the group stage last year. Pegula, meanwhile, will be defending semifinal points.

content.summary: Only 50 days remain until the year-end WTA Finals at Indian Wells. Here's what to watch for, and what's at stake, as we edge close and closer to the premier tournament on the WTA calendar.

content.title: Pegula pulls out of Singapore after busy Hard-Court Swing
content.description: On the heels of her run to the US Open semifinals, Jessica Pegula will miss next week's Singapore Tennis Open. She is projected to return at the end of the month in Beijing.

related.label: Recapping the WTA Americas Coach Inclusion Program's summer; 2026-27 application open now
If the WTA Finals started today: Who's in, on the bubble & outside looking in?
The best moments and biggest takeaways from a memorable US Open

content.body:
Jessica Pegula will miss next week's WTA 500 Singapore Tennis Open Presented by BNP Paribas, she announced on social media.

"I'm really disappointed to have to withdraw from Singapore," Pegula wrote in an Instagram story on Tuesday evening. "After a long and physically demanding few weeks at the US Open, I'm just not quite ready to get back on court and compete at the level I expect from myself.

"I was really looking forward to playing in Singapore and hope I can come back in the future ❤️"

It was quite a busy Hard-Court Swing for Pegula, currently at a career-high No. 3 in the PIF WTA Rankings.

She reached finals in Washington, D.C. and Cincinnati, with a run to the Round of 16 in Toronto sandwiched in between, before reaching the semifinals of the US Open for the second straight year.

The 32-year-old went 15-4 during the American Hard-Court Swing, and her 50 wins lead the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz. She's also currently third on the Race to the WTA Finals leaderboard, with 5,825 points.

Pegula is still scheduled to play the China Open, the first of back-to-back WTA 1000s, at the end of the month.

Pegula was going to be the top seed in Singapore. It will now be World No. 5 Mirra Andreeva. The 28-player field also includes Top 20 players Amanda Anisimova and Alexandra Eala. Maja Chwalinska, Elise Mertens, Barbora Krejcikova and Maria Sakkari will also be in the draw.

The Singapore Tennis Open and Korea Open, also being played next week, are the first two tournaments of the Asian Swing. They each kick off on Sept. 21 and will run through Sept. 27.

From there, the tour will head to Beijing for the China Open, beginning on Sept. 30 and concluding on Oct. 11.

content.body:
Jessica Pegula has long been one of the most entertaining and insightful interviews on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz, mixing sharp insight and intellect with candor and dry humor.

That humor often comes across most in post-match press conferences after disappointing defeats. We saw it in 2022, when she came to the media room with a Heineken after losing to Iga Swiatek in the US Open quarterfinals.

Then at last year's US Open, Pegula posted on X that the tournament's signature cocktail was helping her cope with her crushing semifinal loss to Aryna Sabalenka.

When you lost 4 points on serve in the 3rd but you lost the match pic.twitter.com/KYHqfNBeJR

— Jessie Pegula (@JPegula) September 5, 2025

Pegula had another drink in hand during her press conference on Thursday, following another loss to Sabalenka, but this one wasn't quite as strong.

"I'm always at a US Open press conference trying to pee for doping," she explained when asked what was in her plastic Lavazza cup. "But it's just espresso. Decaf espresso."

When the reporter said he thought it might be tequila, the World No. 3 didn't hate the idea.

"I wish," she said with a smile. "Nobody offered to bring me any. It's coffee this year. But yeah, it's just another night. Another loss and another ... trying to go to the bathroom."

Though Pegula came out on the losing end against the top seed on Thursday, it was another strong Hard-Court Swing the American, who reached finals in Washington, D.C. and Cincinnati before reaching the final four in New York. Her 50 wins currently lead the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz.

As for her 7-5, 6-2 loss to Sabalenka, all Pegula could do was tip her cap to the two-time defending US Open champion.

"I think that's definitely -- you can ask her -- probably the best match she's played this year," she said. "I mean, I thought her level was insanely high. ...I don't know who pissed her off today. Hopefully it wasn't me, but it might have been. I don't know. She played insane. She played a super high level."

Pegula is next scheduled to play the WTA 500 Singapore Open, which begins on Sept. 21.
content.author: Brad Kallet
content.summary: Jessica Pegula has been known to bring a beverage to post-match press conferences at the US Open, and on Thursday evening it was a decaf espresso.

content.title: Sabalenka bests Pegula again in New York to reach fourth straight US Open final
content.description: Aryna Sabalenka defeated Jessica Pegula for the third straight year in New York to reach her fourth straight US Open final. With the win, she became the first player in the Open Era to make eight straight Grand Slam hard‑court finals. She'll face Elena Rybakina for the title.

related.label: Siniakova, Townsend one win away from career Grand Slam at US Open
Dabrowski and Stefani's WTA Finals moment is five years in the making
The long, methodical road that carried Elena Rybakina to No. 1

content.body:
Aryna Sabalenka again had Jessica Pegula's number on Arthur Ashe Stadium, defeating the American No. 1 in straight sets to reach her fourth consecutive US Open final and keep her bid for a three-peat alive.

It's the third straight year Sabalenka has beaten Pegula in New York, this time earning a 7-5, 6-2 victory in 1 hour and 20 minutes. She improved to 10-4 against Pegula in WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz play.

US Open: Scores | Order of play | Draws

"I was super desperate. I lost a tough match on grass against Jess, and I wasn't really performing well in the middle part of the season," Sabalenka said in her post-match press conference. "It kind of feels like for me, talking about Grand Slams, like a last push for the season. I wanted badly to go to the final, and of course I want to go all the way.

"The mentality was just, 'I'm ready. I'm ready for whatever it's going to take to get the win.'"

2023, 2024, 2025, 2026 😤@SabalenkaA is BACK in the US Open final!#USOpen pic.twitter.com/94dPVBlH34

— wta (@WTA) September 11, 2026

With the win, Sabalenka becomes the first player in the Open Era to reach eight consecutive Grand Slam hard-court finals, surpassing the seven in a row achieved by Steffi Graf, Martina Hingis and Novak Djokovic. She is also the sixth woman in the Open Era to reach four or more straight US Open singles finals, joining Evonne Goolagong Cawley, Chris Evert, Martina Navratilova, Graf and Serena Williams.

It marks Sabalenka's ninth Grand Slam final overall. Her opponent will be No. 2 seed Elena Rybakina, whom she has faced twice in Major finals. Sabalenka beat her in the 2023 Australian Open final and lost in three sets in Melbourne earlier this year.

Entering the final in peak form

For someone who lost rather convincingly in a Grand Slam semifinal, Pegula was largely positive in her post-match presser. She chalked it up to Sabalenka playing her best tennis in months.

"That's definitely -- you can ask her -- the best match she's played this year. I thought her level was insanely high," Pegula said. "Maybe she felt a little bit off at the beginning, but I feel like we were both playing well, serving well. I don't know who pissed her off today... hopefully it wasn't me totally, but it might've been.

"I don't know. She played insane. She played at a super high level. Honestly, I don't really know if there was much I could do today."

The first 10 games were tight. They traded holds and generated just one break point each until 5-5. But after Sabalenka held for 6-5, she ripped a backhand a few points later that Pegula couldn't handle, breaking to take the opening set.

The second set told a different story.

Sabalenka converted her fourth break point with a forehand return winner off Pegula's second serve to go up 3-1. Pegula's struggles behind her second serve loomed large -- she won just 5 of 19 (26%) of her second-serve points.

Sabalenka, meanwhile, faced only one break point all night and broke again a few games later to close out a commanding win.

Standing strong 🗽@SabalenkaA powers her way into the US Open final!#USOpen pic.twitter.com/ML5RWFvUKY

— wta (@WTA) September 11, 2026

"I think this season -- especially at the beginning -- I played a lot of incredible matches at a really high level," Sabalenka said. "But today I really performed well. I felt like whatever decision I would make, it was the right decision. So I would definitely say that against Jess today, compared to the last matches we played, it was definitely a better level from me."

Should Sabalenka carry that level into Saturday's final, her chances of claiming a fifth Major title look strong.

content.title: Pegula comes from a break down in third set to make US Open semifinal return
content.description: Jessica Pegula overcame shaky serving to rally past Emma Navarro in three sets and reach her third straight US Open semifinal. The win extended her perfect record against Navarro and sent her into her fourth career Major semifinal.

related.label: Sabalenka escapes Noskova from a break down in decider at US Open
Qualifying for WTA Finals would be a 'dream come true' for Noskova
Marta Kostyuk set to break into WTA Top 10

content.body:
Jessica Pegula didn't have her best stuff Tuesday night in New York -- especially on serve -- but she did what she usually does and found a way through.

The No. 3 seed rallied from a set down and overcame an early third-set deficit to defeat No. 26 seed Emma Navarro 3-6, 6-4, 6-3 in 2 hours and 21 minutes inside a packed Arthur Ashe Stadium, advancing to the US Open semifinals for the third straight year.

US Open: Scores | Order of play | Draws

"It was really tough. It was physical. It was humid. I wasn't exactly serving my best, and I was fighting a lot of demons out there today," Pegula said in her on-court interview. "So thank you guys so much for coming out here. It's an honor to play in front of you guys. There's nothing like it."

It's Pegula's fourth Grand Slam semifinal overall; she also reached the last four at the Australian Open earlier this year.

HEAR HER ROAR 📣

Jessica Pegula battles past Navarro in three sets.#USOpen pic.twitter.com/QaDFpJrAWL

— wta (@WTA) September 9, 2026

The 2024 US Open runner-up improves to 5-0 against Navarro, with three of those wins coming in three sets. Pegula owns the most three-set wins (90) and comeback wins (48) of any WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz player since the start of the decade.

Despite winning just 41% of her second-serve points, Pegula finished with more winners (31) than unforced errors (30) and broke Navarro five times. Neither player found much rhythm throughout, combining for 24 break points.

"It was super back and forth," Navarro said in her post-match press conference. "I think there was a minute where I felt like I kind of had her number. Then she probably felt the same about me for a little while and probably at the right times. I don't know. One of us would get a little bit of momentum, and then the other would step up and play a good point."

One of Pegula's best points came when she flashed quick hands and ripped a crosscourt backhand return winner to break for 4-2 in the decider. She later produced a rare (for the night), high-quality second serve to close out the match and earn her 50th tour-level win of 2026.

Third time's the charm?

Aryna Sabalenka defeated Pegula in straight sets in the 2024 US Open final, then came from a set down to beat her in last year's semifinals. Pegula, who trails the head-to-head 4-9, hopes this year brings a different outcome.

"I think it's fun to look at the rivalry we've had," Pegula said in her post-match press conference. "She's gotten me here the last couple of years. I've been able to beat her a few times, maybe on a smaller stage, so I think that's going to be a hurdle for me to get over.

"But at the same time, I think it's fun. We've challenged each other. I know she's definitely pushed me to become a better player, so I always respect and appreciate that aspect of our rivalry."

Pegula has had her moments recently, winning two of their last three meetings -- a come-from-behind win last year in Wuhan and a three-set victory in the Berlin semifinals earlier this year, where she took the final set 6-0.

But to end the slide against Sabalenka in New York and reach a second Grand Slam final, Pegula knows she'll need even more on Thursday.

"Changing the direction of the ball, not getting too predictable and making her have to move and come up with good shots on the run -- I think that's something I've done really well when I've done well against her," Pegula said. "I think that's going to be key for me.

"She's not going to want me to do that, so it's always a back and forth for both of us. I'm going to draw on those past few matches, but I think I've just been able to play pretty aggressive and get her off balance."

Pegula (70.3%, 71-30) now holds the highest career win rate at Grand Slams of any active player with at least 10 matches played who has not won a Major, surpassing Elina Svitolina (70.0%, 119-51).

content.title: US Open semifinals: Who of the top four will play in the season's last Grand Slam final?
content.description: No. 1 seed Aryna Sabalenka and No. 3 seed Jessica Pegula will play each other for the 14th time while new World No. 1 Elena Rybakina battles No. 4 seed Coco Gauff as all seek a spot in Saturday's US Open final.

related.label: Sabalenka escapes Noskova from a break down in decider at US Open
Pegula comes from a break down in third set to make US Open semifinal return
The long, methodical road that carried Elena Rybakina to No. 1

content.body:
NEW YORK -- We're down to the final four in New York, and it's only fitting the top four seeds will compete for a spot in the 2026 US Open final on Thursday. 

Two-time defending champion and No. 1 seed Aryna Sabalenka and No. 3 seed Jessica Pegula will write the 14th chapter of their rivalry while new World No. 1 Elena Rybakina battles No. 4 seed Coco Gauff for the second time in three tournaments. 

Ahead of Thursday's night session semifinals, here's the case for each of the final four.

History made

Thursday's semifinals will mark the second time in the Open Era that the top four women's seeds have advanced to the US Open semifinals, following 1975 (No. 1 Chris Evert, No. 2 Virginia Wade, No. 3 Martina Navratilova, No. 4 Evonne Goolagong Cawley).

It's also the first time this has occurred at any Grand Slam since Wimbledon in 2009 (No. 1 Dinara Safina, No. 2 Serena Williams, No. 3 Venus Williams, No. 4 Elena Dementieva).

Sabalenka vs. Pegula

Head-to-head: Sabalenka leads 9-4
Last meeting: Pegula def. Sabalenka 6-4, 6-7 (4), 6-0 at 2026 Berlin semifinals
Last hard-court meeting: Sabalenka def. Pegula 4-6, 6-2, 6-3 at 2025 WTA Finals Riyadh group stage

The case for Sabalenka: The quest for the three-peat at Flushing Meadows is going accordingly to plan for Sabalenka, who has recorded her best result since reaching the semifinals at Berlin. For her standards, many of her recent results have not been up to far, but Sabalenka has found a new rhythm and consistent form in New York. 

After four straight sets wins to begin the tournament, she passed a difficult test in Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova, who Sabalenka overcame a third-set break and won in the super tiebreak. Despite the frustrations in the match, Sabalenka seemed to have regain composure, play her game more freely and escape with the win. 

Her biggest key thus far has been blocking the outside noise. She's focused on her own process and hasn't put too much thought on the No. 1 ranking -- which is no longer hers -- or the perception of her game in recent tournaments. She's simply focused on the three-peat. That's something she learned when she had the chance to three-peat at the Australian Open, and though she couldn't achieve it in Melbourne, the lessons have been taken into account here. 

"I'm just super happy that I put myself in the position where I have chance to go for three-peat, even though I'm still far away from that," Sabalenka said. "What I learned from Australia is it's really important to shut down all of the noises and having that on the back of your mind. It's nothing wrong about that, just as long as you're focusing on yourself, as long as you're ready to fight, basically."

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by US Open (@usopen)

The case for Pegula: Pegula's stellar summer continues. After finals in Washington and Cincinnati, Pegula is through to her third straight US Open semifinal still in search of winning that coveted first Grand Slam. It hasn't been the smoothest of paths for Pegula, who went three-sets with 2021 finalist Leylah Fernandez in the third round, but that's expected in a Grand Slam. Tuesday, she edged out fellow American Emma Navarro in a gritty, back-and-forth three-set win, her 50th this season on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz.

Though Sabalenka's summer hasn't been to the level as Pegula's, Pegula is not surprised to see Sabalenka's success at the US Open and she's ready for the latest installment of their rivalry. Their rivalry is what motivates her. Pegula and Sabalenka's last four matchups have gone to a decider, with each taking two apiece.

"I think for me, I'm going to try to pull what I did well from those few matches, but then also be aware that she's a top player," Pegula said. "Her and her team I feel like do a really great job of looking at what they need to improve, what other players are doing against her."

"It's fun to look at the rivalry we've had. She's gotten me here the last couple of years. I have been able to beat her a few times, maybe on a smaller stage, so I think that's going to be kind of a hurdle for me to get over."

Rybakina vs. Gauff

Head-to-head: Tied at 1-1
Last meeting: Rybakina def. Gauff 5-7, 6-2, 6-2 at 2026 Toronto semifinals

The case for Rybakina: The first item on the to-do list was checked off Wednesday as Rybakina's three-set win over Zheng Qinwen secured the Kazakh's seat in the throne of the PIF WTA Rankings -- she's the 30th player to become the World No. 1 since the format was introduced in 1975. 

More importantly, the second item on the to-do list is to win the US Open, which would be Rybakina's third Grand Slam. She's been solid so far, and though -- admittedly -- she wasn't sure she'd play the tournament after an injury scare in Cincinnati, Rybakina has looked dominant. Aside from her quarterfinal, she's won all her matches in straight sets, including a powerful victory of two-time US Open champion Naomi Osaka in the fourth round. 

"I think from where I was coming to this tournament, being injured and not practicing, I think we came pretty far," Rybakina said Wednesday. "Now [it's] just last pushes and important to still enjoy. Hopefully it's going to go my way."

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

As for the new World No. 1, Rybakina is grateful for the recognition but she's strictly focusing on the next match.

"It's a different achievement, and I feel like you're going for the titles more, and then ranking, it might follow up, maybe not. Depends on how others play," Rybakina added. "But mostly you think about the titles in the end of the day, and I'm glad I have two right now. I try my best to win here. If not, of course I will have other chances."

The case for Gauff: You can never count Gauff out. Saving two match points vs. Andreeva in the second set tiebreak, Gauff turned the match around and maintained a perfect 6-0 record against the Roland Garros winner. It was her first dropped set after a stretch of 20 consecutive, a testament to the stellar form the 2023 US Open champion has had this summer. She is now tied with Pegula for 12 comeback wins this season. 

Coming off a title in Cincinnati, Gauff has always said the goal for the Hard-Court Swing is to peak at the US Open, and she has done just that with a prime position to reach another major final. She'll have to overcome Rybakina in what will be Gauff's seventh Grand Slam semifinal, and though their history is brief, she has the home-crowd advantage and all the weapons to test Rybakina. 

"Sometimes you just need a chance, and I think I got my chances today," Gauff said. "I was really determined to not lose that second set because I felt I worked so hard to give myself opportunities and lost them. Once the third set started I felt pretty confident I was going to come out with that one.

content.title: By the numbers: Navarro, Pegula set up first all-American US Open quarterfinal since 2015
content.description: Emma Navarro advanced to the US Open quarterfinals for the second time with a 6-4, 6-2 victory over Anna Kalinskaya on Sunday night. She will face No. 3 seed Jessica Pegula in the first all-American women’s singles quarterfinal at the US Open since 2015.

related.label: Pegula heaps 'respect' on Cirstea after US Open Round of 16 win
Noskova converts sixth match point to oust Kostyuk, reach first US Open quarterfinal
Sabalenka keeps three-peat bid alive with win over Townsend

content.body:
Two years after reaching her first - and so far only - Grand Slam semifinal at the US Open, Emma Navarro is back in the quarterfinals in New York after a straight-sets victory over Anna Kalinskaya on Arthur Ashe Stadium on Sunday night.

The match started with both players holding serve without much trouble through the first nine games of the opening set. The first break-point opportunity came in the 10th game on Kalinskaya’s serve, and Navarro took advantage to take the set 6-4.

With the first set under her belt, Navarro looked more confident as she jumped to a 5-1 lead in the second. Although Kalinskaya, who had won both of their previous meetings, pulled one break back, it was not enough. Navarro broke again in the eighth game to wrap up the 6-4, 6-2 victory in 1 hour, 21 minutes.

Calm. Cool. And Collected.

She gets it from her mom 😅 pic.twitter.com/i5hgKymNTr

— US Open Tennis (@usopen) September 7, 2026

“I know Anna can catch fire and get on a run, and I wanted to just try to break her rhythm as much as I could, and maybe she didn’t play as consistently as she would like to,” Navarro said after her win. “Just proud of my patience and ability to be putting balls in the court and keep asking her the questions.”

After a difficult year navigating health issues, Navarro said she is feeling confident about her game once again.

“I’m feeling good mentally, like feeling resilient, feeling calm, feeling strong,” she said. “So I think that’s a huge part of the game, and yeah, certainly can’t be overlooked. When I’m feeling good mentally, I think good things happen for me.”

Here are some key numbers from Navarro’s win over Kalinskaya:

4: This is Navarro’s fourth career Grand Slam quarterfinal. She previously reached the quarterfinals at Wimbledon 2024, the US Open 2024 and the Australian Open 2025.

9: The number of double faults Kalinskaya hit during the match, along with two aces. Navarro, meanwhile, hit just one double fault and six aces.

24: This was the American's 24th win in a completed Grand Slam match after winning the first set, against just two losses. Those losses came against Barbora Krejcikova at the 2025 US Open and Magda Linette at the 2026 Australian Open.

32: The number of unforced errors from Kalinskaya, compared with just 10 from Navarro. Kalinskaya also hit 17 winners to Navarro’s 15.

40: The number of games Navarro has lost en route to the quarterfinals at this US Open - the most of any player so far at the event. It is also the second-most games conceded en route to a Grand Slam quarterfinal. The 61 games she conceded en route to the 2025 Australian Open quarterfinals were the most by any player reaching a Grand Slam quarterfinal in the Open Era.

Pegula, who leads 4-0 in H2H, awaits in quarterfinals

Up next for Navarro is an all-American quarterfinal against No. 3 seed Jessica Pegula, which will guarantee at least one American woman and one American man in the semifinals of this year’s event.

How good is this!? pic.twitter.com/ocXgXJN3T8

— US Open Tennis (@usopen) September 7, 2026

Pegula has won all four of her career head-to-head meetings against Navarro, including their most recent clash in the round of 32 in Cincinnati last month. This will be the first all-American women’s singles quarterfinal at the US Open since Serena Williams defeated Venus Williams in 2015.

“Jess is really tough,” Navarro said when looking ahead to her next match. “She probably hits the flattest ball on tour, keeps it low, can hit it short and flat or deep and it looks the same. Just a really great ball striker and super consistent from the baseline. I think I’ll have to match that and try to get her out of her rhythm a little bit.

“I have lost to her a few times now, but there’s always that time when you get over the hump and get the win, so hopefully that will be in a couple of days.”

content.title: Pegula heaps 'respect' on Cirstea after US Open Round of 16 win
content.description: No. 3 seed Jessica Pegula reached her fourth US Open quarterfinal in the last five years with a straight-sets win over Sorana Cirstea.

related.label: ‘I felt like I belonged’: Townsend takes stock after falling to Sabalenka
Sabalenka keeps three-peat bid alive with win over Townsend
Noskova converts sixth match point to oust Kostyuk, reach first US Open quarterfinal
Pegula holds off Cirstea in Cincinnati Round of 16 thriller

content.body:
One word was on Jessica Pegula's mind after beating Sorana Cirstea in the Round of 16 of the US Open: respect. 

Facing the 36-year-old No. 16 seed for the second time in the last 18 days, Pegula was a 6-3, 6-4 winner to reach her fourth US Open quarterfinal in the last five years. But she was quick to praise Cirstea after what was ostensibly the final Grand Slam match of the latter's career.

On Cirstea, who plans to retire at season's end, Pegula said "I think she's such a great competitor and the utmost professional."

"I know it seemed somewhat straightforward, but that was a battle," she added. "It was definitely really intense."

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by US Open (@usopen)

The level picked up considerably inside Louis Armstrong Stadium after Pegula won the first 13 points of the match. In their last meeting, on Aug. 19 at the Cincinnati Open, Pegula was up a set and a break before needed to grind through a 6-2, 4-6, 7-5 win -- and she avoided a similar fate on Sunday despite 11 combined breaks of serve by the two players. 

After leading 3-0 to start the match, Pegula held from 0-40 in the sixth game to keep her lead, and needed five set points to take the set. Later in set two, she won four of the first five games -- but held off Cirstea down the stretch. The Romanian saved four break points to hold to trail 4-2, and the match was decided by four straight breaks. 

Pegula later said that if she was the one to close the curtain on Cirstea's efforts on the major stage, she wanted to make sure that the Romanian knew how much she admired not only the way she competed.

"I just told her, I don't know if you're still going to play next year, but you're playing great," she said. 

"I just always like the way she's kind of carried herself, gone about her business," Pegula continued. "I think she's just had a really nice perspective as far as the interviews she's given, especially this year, and why she's playing so well and at a different point in her career and what she's said about that.

"I just kind of always like listening to that side of it, and I think what she says is great and kind of more I can relate to as a player, having a good perspective and enjoying it and enjoying competing and doing what you love."

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

In the final eight, Pegula will face fellow American and No. 26 seed Emma Navarro, who beat No. 21 seed Anna Kalinskaya under the lights in Arthur Ashe Stadium late Sunday.
